metadata.title: On weight initialization in deep neural networks

nodes.name: Weight-initialization variance problem
nodes.statement: The problem can be stated as follows: If the weights in a neural network are initialized using samples from a normal distribution, ${\cal{N}}(0,v^{2})$, how should $v^{2}$ be chosen to ensure that the variance of the outputs from the different layers are approximately the same?
nodes.statement_short: Choose the variance $v^2$ of normal weight initialization so that layer outputs keep equal variance.

nodes.name: Glorot-Bengio initialization for linear activations
nodes.statement: The first systematic analysis of this problem was conducted by Glorot and Bengio \cite{glorot2010understanding} who showed that for a linear activation function, the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer.
conclusions: the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer
nodes.statement_short: For linear activations the optimal weight variance is $1/N$ (fan-in $N$).

nodes.name: Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: Although the paper makes several assumptions about the inputs to the model, it works extremely well in many cases and is widely used in the initialization of neural networks to date; this initialization scheme is commonly referred to as the {\it{Xavier initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: The $v^2 = 1/N$ scheme of Glorot and Bengio is called the Xavier initialization.

nodes.name: He initialization
nodes.statement: In an important follow up paper, He and colleagues \cite{he2015delving} argue that the {\it{Xavier initialization}} does not work well with the RELU activation function, and instead propose an initialization of $v^{2} = 2/N$ (commonly referred to as the {\it{He initialization}}).

nodes.name: He et al. 30-layer network example
nodes.statement: In support of their initialization, they provide an example of a 30 layer neural network which converges with the {\it{He initialization}}, but not under the {\it{Xavier initialization}}.

nodes.name: Why He initialization converges and Xavier does not
nodes.statement: To the best of my knowledge, the precise reason for the convergence of one method and the non-convergence of the other is not fully understood.

nodes.name: Deep neural network layer recursions
nodes.statement: Consider a deep neural network with $M$ layers. The relationship between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer ($x_{m}$) and $m+1^{th}$ layer ($x_{m+1}$) are described by the recursions \be y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij} \enum{in1} \ee and \be x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{g}(y_{m}(i)). \enum{in2} \ee Here $p_{j} = {\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)$, ${\bf{W}}_{m}$ is a matrix of weights for the $m^{th}$ layer, $g$ is the non-linear activation function, and $N$ is the number of nodes in the hidden layers respectively.
nodes.statement_short: An $M$-layer network: $y_m = W_m x_m$ (sum of $p_{ij}$), $x_{m+1} = g(y_m)$, $N$ nodes per hidden layer.

nodes.name: I.i.d. normal weights
nodes.statement: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$.

nodes.name: I.i.d. standardized first-layer inputs
nodes.statement: Consistent with the assumptions in \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving}, I assume that the inputs to the first layer are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

nodes.name: Pre-activation mean and variance $r_m$, $u_m^2$
nodes.statement: For convenience, I use $r_{m}$ and $u_{m}^{2}$ to denote the mean and variance of $y_{m}(i)$ respectively.

nodes.name: Layer-input moments $\mu_m$, $s_m^2$
nodes.statement: Due to the symmetry in the problem, all inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer will have the same means and variances during the first forward pass (i.e., $E(x_{m}(i)) = \mu_m$ and $Var(x_{m}(i)) = s_{m}^{2}$ for all $i$); the covariances between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer need not be 0.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry all inputs to layer $m$ share mean $\mu_m$ and variance $s_m^2$ (covariances may be nonzero).

nodes.name: Variance-preserving initialization goal
nodes.statement: The goal is to find the value of $v^{2}$ which ensures that $s_{1}^{2} \approx s_{2}^{2} ...\approx s_{M}^{2} = 1$ during the first forward pass.
nodes.statement_short: Find $v^2$ with $s_1^2 \approx \dots \approx s_M^2 = 1$ on the first forward pass.

nodes.name: Proposition 1 (independence of weights and layer inputs)
nodes.statement: During the first iteration, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$
conclusions: $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in \eref{in1} and \eref{in2}, $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer. Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$. Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$
nodes.statement_short: Layer inputs are functions of earlier weights and inputs, hence independent of the fresh layer-$m$ weights.

nodes.name: Zero mean of pre-activations (eq. in201)
nodes.statement: Taking expectations in \eref{in1} and using proposition 1, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0$ yields \be r_{m} = E(y_{m}(i)) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E(x_{m}(j)) = 0. \enum{in201} \ee

nodes.name: Expansion of pre-activation variance (eq. in203)
nodes.statement: Therefore, $u_{m}^{2} = Var(y_{m}(i)) = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right) - \left(E(y_{m}(i))\right)^{2} = E\left(y_{m}(i)^{2}\right)$. Using \eref{in1}, \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split} \ee
nodes.statement_short: $u_m^2 = E(y_m^2)$ expanded into diagonal and cross terms.

nodes.name: Vanishing cross terms (eq. in2041)
nodes.statement: From proposition 1, ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ and ${\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)$ will (a) be independent of each other, and (b) be independent of $x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)$. Using these results, along with the fact that $E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)) = 0 $ gives \newline \be E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right) = E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E({\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l))E(x_{m}(j)x_{m}(l)) = 0. \enum{in2041} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Cross terms $E(W_m(i,j)x_m(j)W_m(k,l)x_m(l))$ vanish.

nodes.name: Pre-activation variance formula (eq. in204)
nodes.statement: Plugging \eref{in2041} into \eref{in203} gives \be \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= Nv^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ \enum{in204} \end{split} \ee for all $i$. Interestingly, this result holds for any arbitrary covariance structure of the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer.
assumptions: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$
conclusions: this result holds for any arbitrary covariance structure of the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer
nodes.statement_short: $u_m^2 = N v^2 (s_m^2 + \mu_m^2)$ for any covariance structure of the layer inputs.

nodes.name: Large hidden-layer width
nodes.statement: To answer this question, I make the additional assumption that the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'; this assumption is reasonable given that most neural networks have several hundred nodes in the hidden layers.

nodes.name: Proposition 2 (approximate normality of pre-activations)
nodes.statement: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.
assumptions: the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'
conclusions: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Pre-activations $y_m(i)$ are approximately normal for large width.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$. Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \be \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \ee where the last equality follows from \eref{in2041}. This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}. Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}). Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations.
nodes.statement_short: Show the summands $p_{ij}$ are zero-mean and uncorrelated, then invoke the Central Limit Theorem for large $N$.

nodes.name: First-order Taylor approximation of the activation (eq. in205)
nodes.statement: When $g(x)$ is differentiable at 0, we can perform a Taylor expansion in \eref{in2} about $E(y_{m}(i)) = 0$. Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored, \be x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + (y_{m} - 0)g'(0). \enum{in205} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Linearize: $x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + y_m g'(0)$, dropping higher-order terms.

nodes.name: Mean of next-layer inputs (eq. in206)
nodes.statement: Taking the expectation in \eref{in205} gives \be \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206} \ee
nodes.statement_short: $\mu_{m+1} \approx g(0)$.

nodes.name: Layer-input means equal $g(0)$ (eq. in2061)
nodes.statement: This equation suggests that the expected value of the inputs to the $(m+1)^{th}$ layer has little dependence on the moments of the inputs to the ${m}^{th}$ layer. Using this result recursively suggests that for all layers (barring the first), \be \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Recursively, $\mu_j = g(0)$ for all layers after the first.

nodes.name: Variance recursion for differentiable activations (eq. in207)
nodes.statement: Using \eref{in204} and \eref{in2061}, the variance of $x_{m+1}(i)$ can be computed from \eref{in205} as \be \begin{split} s_{m+1}^{2} = Var(x_{m+1}(i)) &\approx (g'(0))^{2} Var(y_{m}(i)) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ &= N(g'(0))^{2}v^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + g(0)^{2}) . \enum{in207} \end{split} \ee

nodes.name: General weight initialization for activations differentiable at 0
nodes.statement: Using the condition $s_{m}^{2} \approx s_{m-1}^{2} ... = s_{1}^{2} = 1$ along with \eref{in2061} and \eref{in207} gives \be v^{2} = \frac{1}{N(g'(0))^{2}(1+g(0)^{2})}, \enum{in208} \ee \noindent Equation \eref{in208} provide a general weight initialization strategy for any arbitrary differentiable activation function.
assumptions: Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored
conclusions: Equation \eref{in208} provide a general weight initialization strategy for any arbitrary differentiable activation function
nodes.statement_short: For $g$ differentiable at 0, set $v^2 = 1/(N g'(0)^2 (1+g(0)^2))$ to preserve unit variance across layers.

nodes.name: Backward-pass constraint is unnecessary
nodes.statement: In their calculations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving} impose an additional set of constraints to ensure that the variance is maintained even during the backward pass. I believe that this is not required, since the requirement that the variance of the inputs at each layer be the same ensures that the gradient flows through in the backward pass.
nodes.statement_short: Equal forward variances suffice for gradient flow, so no extra backward-pass constraint is needed.

nodes.name: Initialization for the hyperbolic tangent (Xavier)
nodes.statement: For the hyperbolic tangent \be g(x) =\mbox{tanh}(x), \ee we have $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$. Plugging these results in \eref{in208} yields \be v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{tanh1} \ee which is precisely the {\it{Xavier Initialization}}.
conclusions: v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}
which is precisely the {\it{Xavier Initialization}}
nodes.statement_short: For tanh ($g(0)=0$, $g'(0)=1$) the general rule gives $v \approx 1/\sqrt{N}$, i.e. Xavier initialization.

nodes.name: Sequential saturation of tanh layers
nodes.statement: In their analysis of a neural network with the hyperbolic tangent activations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} find that the deeper layers in the neural network have a greater proportion of unsaturated nodes than the shallower layers. As is stated in their paper, `why this is happening remains to be understood'.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Why do deeper tanh layers have more unsaturated units than shallower ones?

nodes.name: Variance shrinkage under uniform Glorot initialization (eq. seq1)
nodes.statement: To explain their finding, I begin by noting that in \cite{glorot2010understanding}, the authors initialize the weights using samples from a uniform distribution $\left(U[-1/\sqrt{N},1/\sqrt{N}]\right)$ having a variance of $1/3N$. Therefore, from \eref{in2061} and \eref{in207}, with $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$, we have $\mu_{m} = 0$ and \be s_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{3}s_{m}^{2} < s_{m}^{2} \ee \enum{seq1} respectively.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: With $U[-1/\sqrt N, 1/\sqrt N]$ weights, $s_{m+1}^2 = s_m^2/3$.

nodes.name: Pre-activation variance decreases with depth
nodes.statement: From \eref{in204}, this implies that $u_{m+1}^{2}<u_{m}^{2}$ for all $m$ (i.e., $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$).
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Density of the tanh transform of a normal variable
nodes.statement: Using results from \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by \be f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1}, \ee where \be t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right). \ee
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
conclusions: $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by
nodes.statement_short: If $y \sim N(0,u^2)$ then $\tanh(y)$ has an explicit pdf in $t_y = \operatorname{artanh}(y)$.

nodes.name: Tanh pdf plots match Glorot-Bengio simulations
nodes.statement: Plots of this pdf for different values of $u_{m}$ (provided in Figure \ref{fig:tanh}) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of \cite{glorot2010understanding} (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure \ref{fig:tanh} and figure 4 of \cite{glorot2010understanding} suggests that $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, as is expected.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Shape of the tanh-transformed normal distribution
nodes.statement: From the results in \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, we expect the activations to be (a) approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0 and (b) bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
conclusions: approximately normally distributed
bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1
nodes.statement_short: tanh of $N(0,u^2)$ is near-normal for small $u$ and bimodal near $\pm1$ for $u$ near 1.

nodes.name: Explanation of sequential saturation
nodes.statement: Accordingly, since $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1), and the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
assumptions: since $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$
conclusions: we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1)
the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network
nodes.statement_short: Since $u_m^2$ shrinks with depth, shallow tanh layers saturate more than deep ones.

nodes.name: Initialization for the sigmoid activation
nodes.statement: For the sigmoid activation defined as \be g(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \mbox{e}^{-x}} \ee we have $g(0) = 0.5$, $g'(0) = 1/4$. Plugging these values in \eref{in208} yields \be v \approx \frac{3.6}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{relur} \ee
assumptions: For the sigmoid activation defined as
conclusions: v \approx \frac{3.6}{\sqrt{N}}
nodes.statement_short: For the sigmoid ($g(0)=1/2$, $g'(0)=1/4$) the general rule gives $v \approx 3.6/\sqrt{N}$.

nodes.name: CIFAR-10 sigmoid experiment: Xavier vs. proposed initialization
nodes.statement: To compare the initialization described in \eref{relur} with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, I use a simple 10 layer neural network whose architecture is described in Figure \ref{fig:nnarch}. For my experiments, I use the CIFAR 10 dataset \cite{krizhevsky2009learning} comprising 60,000, $32 \times 32$ color images evenly split over 10 classes. The dataset comprises 50,000 training examples (which forms the training dataset in my analyses) and 10,000 test examples (which forms the validation dataset in my analyses). \begin{figure} \centering \begin{minipage}{.3\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[width=.5\linewidth]{Figure2ap3.png} \captionof{figure}{Architecture of deep nural network used in analysis of sigmoid; stride lengths in all layers are $2 \times 2$.} \label{fig:nnarch} \end{minipage} \hfill \begin{minipage}{.6\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[width=1\linewidth]{Figure2} \captionof{figure}{Convergence comparison of {\it{Xavier initialization}} with initialization recommended in \eref{relur}. The {\it{Xavier initialization}} stalls while the initialization recommended in \eref{relur} converges proceeds rapidly towards convergence.} \label{fig:conv} \end{minipage} \end{figure} First, I train the neural network with the {\it{Xavier initialization}} for 10 iterations and compute the top 5 accuracy on the validation dataset for each iteration. Next, I repeat the process using the initialization stated in \eref{relur}. A comparison of the validation accuracies for the 2 cases is provided in Figure \ref{fig:conv}, which shows that the convergence appears to stall with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, but proceeds rapidly with the initialization proposed in \eref{relur}.
nodes.statement_short: On a 10-layer sigmoid CNN on CIFAR-10, Xavier stalls while $v \approx 3.6/\sqrt N$ converges quickly.

nodes.name: Mean of RELU outputs (eq. relu1)
nodes.statement: To proceed, I use proposition 2 and \eref{in201} which state that for the first iteration, $ y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$. The mean will be given by \be \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1} \ee
nodes.statement_short: For RELU, $\mu_{m+1} = u_m/\sqrt{2\pi}$.

nodes.name: Second moment of RELU outputs (eq. relu2)
nodes.statement: Similarly, \be E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2} \ee

nodes.name: Variance of RELU outputs (eq. relu3)
nodes.statement: Using \eref{relu1} and \eref{relu2}, \be s_{m+1}^{2} = E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) - \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2} - \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2\pi} \approx 0.34u_{m}^{2}. \enum{relu3} \ee
nodes.statement_short: For RELU, $s_{m+1}^2 = u_m^2/2 - u_m^2/(2\pi) \approx 0.34 u_m^2$.

nodes.name: Required pre-activation variance for RELU (eq. relu301)
nodes.statement: For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 1$ which yields \be u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301} \ee
nodes.statement_short: Unit output variance requires $u_m^2 \approx 3$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the He initialization for RELU
nodes.statement: Plugging \eref{relu301} in \eref{relu1} yields $\mu_{m+1} \approx 0.7$. By the symmetry of the problem during the first iteration, we expect $\mu_{m+1} \approx \mu_{m} ... \approx \mu_{2} \approx 0.7$. Using this result in \eref{in204} yields \be 3 = Nv^{2}(1+ 0.49) \ee or \be v^{2}\approx 2/N, \ee which is consistent with that obtained by \cite{he2015delving}.
assumptions: Since the RELU activation is not differentiable at 0
For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 1$
conclusions: v^{2}\approx 2/N
which is consistent with that obtained by \cite{he2015delving}
nodes.statement_short: For RELU, preserving unit variance forces $v^2 \approx 2/N$, recovering the He initialization.

nodes.name: He et al. 22- and 30-layer RELU networks under Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: In \cite{he2015delving} paper, the authors provide an example of a 22 layer neural network using RELU activations which converges with the {\it{Xavier Initialization}}, and a 30 layer neural network which does not converge with the same initializations and activation functions.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Pre-activation variance under Xavier initialization (eq. r01)
nodes.statement: To understand why this happens, I compute the central moments of $x_{m+1}$ in terms of the central moments of $x_{m}$ when $v^{2} = 1/N$. From \eref{in204} we have \be u_{m}^{2} = s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}. \enum{r01} \ee
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Mean recursion for RELU under Xavier (eq. r02)
nodes.statement: Plugging results from \eref{r01} into \eref{relu1} yields the recursion \be \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{2\pi}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \approx 0.16(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{r02} \ee
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Variance recursion for RELU under Xavier (eq. relu5)
nodes.statement: Similarly, plugging results from \eref{r01} and \eref{r02} in \eref{relu3} yields \be s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 0.34(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{relu5} \ee
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Geometric decay of layer moments for RELU with Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: Simple manipulations of equations \erefs{r01}{relu5} gives \be \mu_{m}^{2} \approx 0.16 \times (0.51)^{m-1} \enum{relu603} \ee and \be s_{m}^{2} \approx 0.34 \times (0.51)^{m-1}. \enum{relu602} \ee for all $m \geq 1$.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.
nodes.statement_short: Under Xavier init with RELU, $\mu_m^2$ and $s_m^2$ decay geometrically like $(0.51)^{m-1}$.

nodes.name: Agreement with CS231n simulations
nodes.statement: These approximations are remarkably accurate, as is demonstrated by comparisons with the simulation experiments described in Figure \ref{fig:cs231ncomp}.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.

nodes.name: Xavier initialization degrades with depth for RELU
nodes.statement: Equation \eref{relu602} shows that the variance of the inputs to the deeper layers is exponentially smaller than the variance of the inputs to the shallower layer. Therefore, the deeper the neural network, the worse the performance of the {\it{Xavier Initialization}} will be.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.
conclusions: the variance of the inputs to the deeper layers is exponentially smaller than the variance of the inputs to the shallower layer
the deeper the neural network, the worse the performance of the {\it{Xavier Initialization}} will be
nodes.statement_short: Input variance shrinks exponentially with depth, so Xavier performs worse in deeper RELU networks.

nodes.name: Explanation of the 22- vs 30-layer convergence gap
nodes.statement: From \eref{relu602}, $s_{22}^{2} \approx 1.62 \times 10^{-7}$ and $s_{30}^{2} \approx 6.33 \times 10^{-10}$. Thus the variance in the input to the $30^{th}$ layer will be $(0.51)^{8} = 3 \times 10^{-3}$ times smaller than the variance to the $22^{nd}$ layer, and explains the possible reason why the 30 layer neural network described in \cite{he2015delving} converges, but the 22 layer neural network does not.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.
conclusions: the variance in the input to the $30^{th}$ layer will be $(0.51)^{8} = 3 \times 10^{-3}$ times smaller than the variance to the $22^{nd}$ layer
nodes.statement_short: The 30th-layer input variance is ~$3\times10^{-3}$ of the 22nd's, explaining the depth-dependent convergence failure.

nodes.name: General initialization for non-differentiable activations
nodes.statement: Given the sharp increase in non-differentiable activation functions over the years, a more general version of my (largely incomplete) analysis of non-differentiable functions is warranted.

nodes.name: Express layer inputs via the recursions
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in \eref{in1} and \eref{in2}, $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer.
nodes.statement_short: Write $x_m(k)$ as a function of earlier-layer weights and first-layer inputs.

nodes.name: Independence of fresh weights
nodes.statement: Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Functions of independent quantities stay independent of the layer-$m$ weights.

nodes.name: Extend to products of inputs
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$
nodes.statement_short: Extend independence to products $x_m(k)x_m(l)$.

nodes.name: Zero mean of summands
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Each summand $p_{ij}$ has mean zero.

nodes.name: Summands are uncorrelated
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \be \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \ee where the last equality follows from \eref{in2041}.
nodes.statement_short: Covariances of distinct summands vanish by eq. in2041.

nodes.name: Apply the Central Limit Theorem
nodes.statement: This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}.
nodes.statement_short: Treat summands as i.i.d. and apply the CLT for large $N$.

nodes.name: Weaker CLT conditions for dependent summands
nodes.statement: Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}).
nodes.statement_short: A CLT for dependent, non-identical summands needs only weak conditions.

nodes.name: Conclude approximate normality
nodes.statement: Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $y_m(i)$ is approximately normal.
